headline: High risk of shared-filesystem prompt injection and data leakage; Gemini CLI’s default filesystem/network access can amplify ctx’s file-observing workflow.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code events and touches filesystem/MCP servers, while Gemini CLI reads repo files and user-provided directories by default. That creates a plausible shared-file bridge where attacker-controlled content in files can be treated as instructions. The interaction is documented only indirectly, so uncertainty pushes severity up from low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or repo files
IF ctx forwards observed file content into downstream prompts or MCP events
IF Gemini CLI processes those files as trusted instructions
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different directories
Disable automatic ingestion of untrusted files
Add a manual review step before any file-derived prompt is sent
Use read-only mounts for ctx observations
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all file-derived content

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch filesystem content, and Gemini CLI explicitly reads repo files and user-provided directories while also using broad network egress. ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and MCP servers. If sensitive material lands in the shared workspace, Gemini CLI can transmit it outward; the pairwise leakage path is plausible in default use, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF sensitive data is present in the shared repo or cwd
IF Gemini CLI is allowed to send context to its backend
IF ctx writes logs or graph data into the same workspace
mitigations: Keep sensitive files outside the shared workspace
Restrict Gemini CLI to non-sensitive directories
Turn off or minimize logging in ctx
Review outbound API destinations before use
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data classification filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx supports multiple instances and uses filesystem/MCP hooks, while Gemini CLI can write the filesystem, modify git state, and supports multiple instances with shared state via filesystem and git only. That is a direct overlapping-write conflict on the same mutable resources, and the default setup is dangerous because concurrent edits can clobber each other.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same git checkout
IF both are allowed to write files or commit changes
IF no external locking or serialization is enabled
mitigations: Run only one writer per checkout
Use separate branches for each agent
Enable file locks around shared outputs
Pause one agent before the other edits git state
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code events and Gemini CLI can act on tool-approved prompts, so Gemini may treat ctx-produced artifacts as authoritative inputs. However, the profiles do not prove an automatic action chain or that Gemini blindly trusts ctx, so this is an inferred medium-risk cascade rather than high.
conditions: IF ctx-generated summaries are fed into Gemini CLI prompts
IF Gemini CLI is instructed to act on those summaries without verification
IF the resulting actions include shell or git operations
mitigations: Require human review of ctx outputs before reuse
Ask Gemini CLI to cite source files before acting
Split analysis and action into separate sessions
Disable auto-execution of tool suggestions
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not state a residency, certification, or retention mismatch. The only concrete compliance-relevant difference is that Gemini CLI handles a Google API key and broad API egress, while ctx touches audit/runtime logs; that suggests possible policy friction, but no specific violation is documented. The other agent is cited because the risk is pairwise logging/egress overlap.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared workspace
IF outbound API use is not approved for that data class
IF logs retain sensitive content beyond policy
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared sessions
Check retention settings before use
Rotate or protect API keys
Redact logs after each run
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
